entries.title: Attacker Control and Impact for Confidentiality and Integrity
entries.venue: Logical Methods in Computer Science, 7(3), 2011 (extended from CSF 2007)

verified.notes: Full HTML text read from arXiv:1107.5594v1; all definitions, theorems, type rules, and examples inspected

entries.closest_relation: characterises attacker influence over trusted computation; relevant to delegation/disclosure exploitation

relevance.useful_parts: Attacker control/impact framework; robust declassification as release control ⊆ attacker control; checked endorsement construct; security type system with trusted-context declassification; irrelevant-attacks exclusion mechanism for endorsement safety
key_findings: Defines attacker knowledge as the set of initial memories compatible with low observations; monotonic — knowledge only shrinks as more low events are produced
Attacker control (Def 9) = set of attacks similar to a given attack in their influence on knowledge; two attacks are similar if they produce the same release events in the same order
Robust declassification (Def 13) = release control ⊆ attacker control at the next release event; intuition: all attacks leading to a release must produce the SAME release event
Endorsement (Section 5) extends robustness by excluding irrelevant attacks — those that disagree at endorsement events — from the robustness check

Checked endorsement (Section 7): conditional trust upgrade 'endorse(x) if e then c1 else c2'; can be translated to direct endorsements for well-typed programs (Proposition 2); the checked endorsement must endorse both the variables AND the check expression

Attacker impact (Definition 24, Section 8) = dual of attacker knowledge: set of attacks matching trusted events (assignments to trusted variables); integrity robustness = attacker can't influence which trusted events occur

4-level security lattice: (P,T), (P,U), (S,T), (S,U) — public/secret × trusted/untrusted; all levels are meaningful (e.g., secret+untrusted = information depends on both secret and attacker-controlled values)

Type system: T-ASGMT requires declassification only in trusted context (pc ⊑ (P,T)); T-ENDORSE requires trusted pc and trusted result variable; T-HOLE restricts attacker code to public contexts (pc ⊑ (P,U))
Progress-sensitive and progress-insensitive variants for both termination-sensitive and insensitive security
Published in LMCS (journal extension of CSF 2007 conference paper); all theorems proved
limitations: Uses scalar 4-level lattice (P/S × T/U), not named principal identities
No connection to an existing organisational ACS — policies are program-level, not enterprise-level
No treatment of LLM agents, prompt injection, or argument-level provenance
No verification of the security layer under arbitrary model proposals
The checked endorsement construct is the closest classical analogue to Conflux delegation, but it endorses variable values, not principal authority

novelty_impact.qualification_needed: The attacker-control/impact framework directly applies to Conflux's exceptions to monotonicity (delegation, disclosure, consent). Conflux should acknowledge that checked endorsement is the closest classical analogue to scoped delegation, but note that it endorses variable values, not principal authority derived from an existing ACS.

entries.title: Progent: Programmable Privilege Control for LLM Agents

verified.notes: arXiv abstract read; v3 (14 May 2026) confirmed

entries.closest_relation: direct challenge; borrow argument policies and expansion lattice
entries.mechanism: DSL over tools/arguments; SMT expansion check; approval

novelty_impact.qualification_needed: Progent mediates tool calls with symbolic policy and argument-sensitive controls; Conflux's argument-level authority should be positioned against this precedent

relevance.useful_parts: Privilege control via symbolic rules over tool names and arguments; SMT solver for monotonic confinement; deterministic policy checking
key_findings: Progent represents privilege as symbolic rules over tool names and arguments; every tool call is checked against the policy through a deterministic procedure
Monotonic confinement: policy updates are SMT-determined as narrowing (auto-applied) or expansion (requires explicit approval); effective action space can only shrink without approval
LLM generates initial policy from user task and updates during execution; prevents silent privilege escalation even with adversarial inputs
Evaluated on AgentDojo and ASB; demonstrated in LangChain and OpenAI Agents SDK
Argument-sensitive policy is directly comparable to Conflux's trusted argument roles
limitations: No principal identities or provenance for authority derivation
Policy is task-specific, not derived from existing organisational ACS
No verification of the security layer under arbitrary model proposals
No argument-level provenance tracking

entries.title: Robust Declassification
entries.venue: Proceedings of the 14th IEEE Computer Security Foundations Workshop, 15-23

verified.notes: Scholar verified; Cornell page confirmed; full text not inspected in this session

entries.closest_relation: attacker cannot manipulate declassification; directly relevant to prompt injection

relevance.useful_parts: Robust declassification condition: attacker cannot manipulate what/when trusted code declassifies; directly relevant to prompt injection
key_findings: Robust declassification asks whether an attacker can influence the decision to declassify — directly relevant to prompt injection
A trusted user may be authorised to release information, but an attacker-authored document should not gain the ability to influence the LLM into exercising that authority
A future disclosure rule should ask both whether release is authorised and which principals may influence the decision to perform it
Provides stronger formal vocabulary for attacker-influence conditions than an entirely new Conflux-specific concept
limitations: Conflux does not yet implement a robustness condition for disclosure
No treatment of LLM agents specifically
No connection to existing ACS
Robust disclosure is listed as future work in SLED-V property hierarchy

novelty_impact.qualification_needed: Concept is directly applicable; Conflux has not yet implemented the corresponding mechanism, so no novelty conflict exists

entries.title: Language-Based Information-Flow Security
entries.venue: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications, 21(1), 5-19

verified.notes: DOI verified; metadata confirmed against IEEE Xplore

entries.closest_relation: vocabulary for explicit/implicit flows, overapproximation, and IFC enforcement

relevance.useful_parts: Vocabulary for explicit/implicit flows, static/dynamic enforcement, noninterference, precision vs soundness; three-way distinction between security provenance, exposure, and attribution
key_findings: Provides the standard vocabulary for language-based IFC: explicit vs implicit flows, termination/timing channels, overapproximation vs exact influence
Conflux's 'influence' is an intentional overapproximation in Sabelfeld-Myers terms: if information from a principal reaches an execution, that principal may influence its output
The three-way distinction (security provenance / exposure measurement / causal attribution) maps to IFC concepts of soundness, precision, and knowledge
Declassification is treated as a controlled exception to noninterference, with dimensions (what, who, where, when)
limitations: Language-based IFC, not agent-level security
No connection to existing organisational ACS
No treatment of LLM agents or prompt injection
Focuses on program-level enforcement, not system-level mediation

novelty_impact.qualification_needed: Conservative label/flow propagation is standard IFC practice; Conflux's overapproximation of influence should be acknowledged as consistent with IFC conventions

key_findings: SecAlign uses preference optimization: constructs dataset with prompt-injected inputs, secure outputs (respond to legitimate instruction), insecure outputs (respond to injection)
Reduces success rates of various prompt injections to <10%, even against sophisticated attacks
Generalizes well against unknown attacks not seen during training
Model-level defence; similar utility to undefended model
Published at ACM CCS 2025; open-source code available
limitations: Model-level defence, not system-level security mechanism
No complete mediation — only prevents instruction following from injected data
No principal provenance or ACS connection
White-box attacks (attention-based) can bypass with 85-95% success rate
Empirical robustness only, not formal guarantee
